title: Why I wrote Towards Deep Tech in Africa
summary: A laboratory key, a question I carried through Dutch clean rooms, and why the book is about building gates on purpose.
body:
By the time I was in the second to the last year of primary school, four people had already decided my future, and none of them agreed. What actually happened had nothing to do with any of them. We moved to a different neighbourhood in Otukpo, and somebody started building a school down the road.

In the second to the last year of that school, I was made laboratory and library prefect. It sounds like nothing. But that key is the single most valuable object anyone has ever handed me, because it meant that the laboratory and the library were open to me whenever I wanted them.

Nobody gave me curiosity. Nobody installed ambition in me, or grit, or a work ethic. I had all of that before the school was built, and so did the boys and girls at the schools down the road. What I was given was a key. **The difference between me and a hundred equally hungry children was not talent. It was access.**

## A question that would not leave

After my master's I moved to the Netherlands and spent the next several years working inside the machine I had read about as a teenager: extreme ultraviolet systems at ASML, carbon capture at Skytree, subsea sensors at Nortek, and the world's first autonomous robotic phlebotomy device at Vitestro.

And the whole time, one question kept circling me. Why do we not have this at home? What, precisely, is wrong?

Not rhetorically. I had studied alongside too many capable, hungry Nigerians to believe the answer was ability or appetite. So I took a doctorate to find out, comparing deep tech ecosystems in Nigeria and the Netherlands across six years of data and twenty-two long interviews with founders, investors, academics and policymakers.

## What I found

Every gap I measured was real, and some of them were enormous. Yet none of them was the whole of what was holding Nigerian builders back. The people I interviewed kept moving the problem to places my numbers did not reach.

When I saw that, I recognised it, because I had lived it. At every point where my life turned, what turned it was a gate opening. Every one of those gates opened by luck. Not one of them was designed. A continent with hundreds of millions of young people cannot run on that.

> If access is what decides who builds, and access arrives by accident, then we are leaving our future to chance and calling the survivors talented.

This book is about building those gates on purpose.

## A reason is not an excuse

There are real reasons why building deep tech in Africa is hard, and I have documented them. But there is a difference between a reason and an excuse, and the difference is entirely in what you do next. A reason describes the wall. An excuse is what you say when you decide not to look for the door.

I want the young engineer in Minna or Kumasi or Kigali, reading with a laptop and a bad connection, to finish the book and understand something specific: that the thing standing between you and the frontier is usually a gate, that gates are built by people, and that you are permitted to build them.

*Towards Deep Tech in Africa: Building the Ground We Stand On* comes out in January 2027. You can [read the full Preface and "A Note on Words" free](/book/sample).
